segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Cinema at once created and fed an appetite for spectacle, offering the chance to recreate the past, reimagine the present and envision the future. The pioneers of this art were not to be found in Hollywood, which at the time did not even exist as a center of film production, but in Europe. Among the most notable were the French filmmakers Georges Méliès (1861-1938), Charles Pathé (1863-1957) and Ferdinand Zecca (1864-1947).

segments.original: We can mention other names that were unknown until then: Thomas Edison (1847-1931), W.K.L Dickson (1854-1932), Louis Le Prince (1841-1890) and Francis Doublier (1878-1948). All of them contributed in some way to the creation of the so-called seventh art, and for that reason we cannot say it was created by a single person, nor does it have a precise date of birth. In 1884, George Eastman invented roll film. In the same decade, Thomas Edison and his assistant W. K. L. Dickson invented the kinetoscope. Many other inventions emerged in parallel or built upon earlier ones.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: After attending the first public screenings of the Lumière brothers' films in 1895, theater producer and magician Georges Méliès quickly recognized cinema's potential as a vehicle for illusion and fantasy. Méliès's signature was his love of illusionism, blending the fantastic with the macabre. The silent film L'Homme à la tête de caoutchouc (The Man with the Rubber Head, 1901) features Méliès as a scientist who attaches a rubber tube to his own severed head to inflate it with a bellows. The experiment is then repeated by one of his assistants, who inflates the head until it explodes.

Phalke (1870-1944), enchanted by one of the first film versions of the life of Christ, learned the rudiments of filmmaking in order to make Raja Harishchandra (1913). This elaborate period drama, based on Hindu mythology, marks the beginning of the Indian film industry.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: In the United States, The Great Train Robbery (1903), directed by Edwin S. Porter (1870-1941), is considered the first American film with a narrative. Porter's innovative shooting and editing techniques, his location shots and the Western format made it extremely thrilling for audiences of the time. As technology advanced, directors were able to make longer films, sometimes turning to literature for inspiration.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: As technology advanced, the length of films increased, making possible the emergence of serial films. One of the most successful examples of the format is the Fantômas series (1913-1914), divided into five parts and based on one of the most popular characters in French crime fiction, played by René Navarre (1877-1968). Directed by Louis Feuillade (1873-1926), each part ran about an hour and always ended on a cliffhanger. The prolific French director also made Les Vampires (The Vampires, 1915). The suspense techniques developed by Feuillade would later influence masters such as Fritz Lang (1890-1976) and Alfred Hitchcock (1899-1980).

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Between 1908 and 1920, cinema developed through so-called serial films, or serials, which became the main attraction of movie houses. This innovation, however, was not an invention of cinema, since at the time, especially in France, biweekly installments of crime and adventure stories were popular and had spread throughout Europe. It was in France, therefore, that the serial was born, with Nick Carter in le roi des détectives, in 1908, based on those installments and directed by Victorin Jasset, an imaginative director who often improvised the script during shooting. Following the series' success, several imitations were made in Europe, such as Raffles and Sherlock Holmes in Denmark, and Nick Carter in Germany.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Serials became very popular among children and young people in the first half of the 20th century, and film screenings, including in Brazil, were generally preceded by an episode of a serial until the '60s, as they were known back then. They were later acquired by TV channels and shown in weekly or daily episodes. Most were Westerns, but there was a wide range of genres: dramas, science fiction, espionage, jungle adventures, as well as book adaptations.

tracks.title: The first film with some underwater sequences

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The opportunity to make longer films, the rise of the Hollywood studios and bigger budgets encouraged filmmakers to produce literary adaptations such as 20,000 Leagues Under the Sea (1916), directed by Stuart Paton (1883-1944) and based on the 1869 novel by Jules Verne, whose book The Mysterious Island (1874) was also adapted for the screen. Paton joined forces with two other British immigrants in the United States, the brothers John and George Williamson, to create the first film with some underwater sequences.

segments.original: The appetite for spectacle continued to be explored in epics such as The Ten Commandments (1923) and Ben-Hur: A Tale of the Christ (1925), forming what would later be known as the sword-and-sandal genre. The latter proved a troubled and expensive production for Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, which had just completed its merger. To make the chariot race more exciting, the studio offered a $100 prize to the winner, and the terrible crash that resulted remained in the film's final cut. The spirit of pioneering director Georges Méliès can be glimpsed in these 1920s epics and, later, in the special effects created by Ray Harryhausen in the 1950s and 1960s. Filmmaking techniques grew more complex and narrative structures increasingly sophisticated, yet cinema's creative foundation — reinventing and reinterpreting reality — has remained a constant since its earliest days.
